title: fosuns clubmed spinoff looks hard sell 2026 09 04
author: Ka Sing Chan
text:
HONG KONG, Sept 4 (Reuters Breakingviews) - Fosun International (0656.HK)
, opens new tab
 will have to work hard for its ClubMed spinoff. Just a year after taking its tourism ​unit that included the resort chain private, it is now relisting
, opens new tab
 ClubMed as a standalone business. That's ‌sensible. But bagging a similar valuation as faster-growing, more profitable rivals will be tough.
The biotech-to-financial-services conglomerate bought ClubMed over a decade ago and folded the business into its broader Fosun Tourism Group, spanning hotels and vacation properties. But FTG's 2018 Hong Kong stock market ​debut was followed by the Covid-19 pandemic and China's property crash. Last year, Fosun bought out the ​rest of FTG at a $1.2 billion valuation — roughly half of what it was worth ⁠at its IPO.
ClubMed is now returning to public markets in an IPO that could raise more than $500 million, according ​to Reuters. The business operates 69 resorts across 40 countries and regions. Its model of leasing most of its properties ​means it is also relatively asset light.
That should help ClubMed market itself as a global hospitality brand. The company reported €57 million ($67 million) of net profit in the first half of the year. Annualise that, and put it on the average 23.5 times price-to-earnings multiple peers ​including Marriott International (MAR.O)
, opens new tab
 and Hilton Worldwide (HLT.N)
, opens new tab
 trade on, per Visible Alpha, and ClubMed's market value could be worth $3 ​billion.
Yet that will be a tough sell. Revenue, of which over half comes from Europe, Middle East and Africa, increased just 1.3% ‌in ⁠2025 and stagnated in the first half. Operating income has been in decline, falling to €160 million last year, down from €181 million in 2023. Higher operating expenses are to blame, as the company upgraded its hotels to include premium all-inclusive services like activities, transportation, childcare and more. That strategy is less profitable as well: ClubMed's 20% EBITDA margin last ​year was well below the ​30% at Hilton.
Focusing on ⁠outbound travellers from the People's Republic makes sense, given ClubMed's parent. But that will be tricky: overseas spending from Chinese tourists grew just 1.4% last year to $254 billion, despite ​a 15% rise in overseas trips, per government data. ClubMed will have to convince ​both holiday-makers and ⁠investors that it's worth the price.
